 📐 **Day 15 Development Log**

💣 Main challenge: Loading T.rex as an icon on a map, indicating reconstructed fossils where they lived in deep time.

🗺️ Approach: Download T. rex as a .png file, then get it to replace the dark-green dots representing reconstructed T.rex fossils in deep time.
             Sounds simple, right?

🤼‍ Challenges(-) & Technical Wins(+):
 - T.rex silhouettes exist all around the net. But many of them required licences.  
   + Asked AI to generate a T.rex silhouette, then sent it to myself.
 - The T.rex art came in .jpeg form
   + Converted it into a .png format with an online converter, asking to make it _transparent_. 
     I wanted the background transparent, as otherwise the background would clip out patches of the world map in the output.
     This would later turn out to be a mistake.
 - After t_rex.png was moved into 'assets\\t_rex.png', was told that no such file existed in the directory. Suspected path-ing issue.
   + Changed directory in code, using:
	BASE_DIR   = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(__file__)) # Go up one level in the directory
	ASSETS_DIR = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "assets")
	T_REX_ICON = mpimg.imread(os.path.join(ASSETS_DIR, "t_rex.png"))
 - This succeeded, but another error arose: Expected a projection subclass. Cannot handle <Geodetic> in imshow()
   + Explained: imshow() expects data already in the map's coordinate system. 
     By using
	ax.imshow(
    	 T_REX_ICON,
   	 extent=[lon - d, lon + d, lat - d, lat + d],
   	 transform=ccrs.Geodetic(),
    	 alpha=0.8 if original else 1.0,
    	 zorder=10
	)
     ...I was changing the coordinate system. My GeoAxes use PlateCarree and I transformed them to Geodetic. This did not work. 
     So I removed the line "transform=ccrs.Geodetic()".
     This would later turn out to be a mistake.
 - My map loaded without code errors. BUT the fossils were MISSING. What happened?
   Some candidate explanations:
   * T.rex image too big
   * T.rex image too small
   * T.rex image (actual .png file) transparent
   * Something wrong with the projection
   * T.rex image buried under other layers (unlikely since this was not an issue before with the dot markers for fossils)
   These possibilities only seemed obvious in retrospect. At the time, it was unclear what the issue was since fossils were not displaying.

   Therefore went by process of elimination:
   + Scaled up T. rex size by 1 order of magnitude, then 2. Still not visible. Unlikely that image was too small.
   + Inserted argument "origin=upper" in ax.imshow(). No change.
   + Inserted quick brute force test:
	import numpy as np

	print("Shape:", T_REX_ICON.shape)
	print("Min/Max:", np.min(T_REX_ICON), np.max(T_REX_ICON))
	print("Unique sample:", np.unique(T_REX_ICON.reshape(-1, T_REX_ICON.shape[-1])[:20], axis=0))
     which gave the output:
        Shape: (1024, 1024, 4)
	Min/Max: 0.0 1.0
	Unique sample: [[0. 0. 0. 0.]]
     T.rex icons still did not show.
   => perhaps there was something wrong with the .png file. Output indicated the .png was 100% transparent.
   + Returned to the original image and used another site to remove the background, and convert it into a .png. This worked!
 - The "brute force test" now worked, and gave the output:
   	Shape: (1024, 1024, 3)
	Min/Max: 0.0 1.0
	Unique sample: [[0.7058824  0.67058825 0.6117647 ]
 	[0.70980394 0.6745098  0.6156863 ]
 	[0.7137255  0.6784314  0.61960787]
 	[0.7137255  0.6901961  0.6431373 ]
 	[0.7176471  0.69411767 0.64705884]
 	[0.72156864 0.6862745  0.627451  ]
 	[0.7254902  0.6901961  0.6313726 ]
 	[0.7294118  0.69411767 0.63529414]
 	[0.7372549  0.7019608  0.6431373 ]
 	[0.7411765  0.7058824  0.64705884]
 	[0.7490196  0.7137255  0.654902  ]
 	[0.7529412  0.7176471  0.65882355]]  
   But the T.rex images were still not showing!
   => This is where the projection error came back to bite me.
   + Added the argument transform=ccrs.Robinson to ax.imshow, the same as my map display projection.
 - The argument transform=ccrs.Robinson to ax.imshow did NOT work...
   ...as the extent=[lon-d, lon+d, lat-d, lat+d], x-axis = longitude and y-axis = latitude, is PlateCarree space, not Robinson space
   ...meaning: the coordinate system that the data lives in (PlateCarree/Geodetic) is NOT THE SAME as the visual projection onto the map!
   => the transform should always be set to the coordinate system of my data! (lon, lat) values are meaningless in Robinson space!
   + changed the argument to transform=ccrs.PlateCarree 
 - Error: Using image transforms requires pykdtree or scipy
   + Downloaded scipy and pykdtree.
 - Error: No module named scipy. But I already downloaded it. Furthermore, ONE T.rex icon showed, but the rest were missing.
   => Realised I was running in multiple Python environments. The first run used environment A (SciPy installed), while the second run used environment B (no SciPy)
   + Made sure to download scipy and pykdtree to EXACTLY the Python environment my notebook used.
     I could identify this Python environment using:
	import sys
	print(sys.executable)
     in Jupyter, to yield the full path.
     Then I opened a cmd window and pasted: "<FULL_PATH_FROM_sys.executable>" -m pip install scipy

... 🔥🔥🔥🔥🔥 AND MY CODE WORKKKKKEEEDDDDD 🔥🔥🔥🔥🔥

🦖🦖🦖 T REXES WERE SHOWING 🦖🦖🦖

Now all that remained was visual cleanup:
 - Too difficult to distinguish between original and reconstructed fossils, since they were both Big T.Rexes.
   + Changed present-day fossils back to grey dots using conditional statements in plot_fossils()
 - Too many T.Rexes... 73 of them...
   + Cut number of T.Rexes down to 4. This also sped up loading by a lot.

💡 Insights: 
 - When an error arises, there can be multiple causes. This can come from any stage of the pipeline, from the environment, 
   from the data source (in this case, an image), from the projection, from coordinate transformations, invalid arguments/functions...
   The key here is to keep a cool head. 
   Then test to eliminate possible causes.
   Once you eliminate the impossible, what remains must be the Truth.
 - Coordinate transformations are proving to be tricky for this pipeline. For that matter, data types (e.g. geometry features)
   are constantly being transformed in various ways. 
   It may be helpful to track the state and type of throughput in this pipeline at each stage, AND
   what can or cannot be done to the data at each stage. What functions apply? What functions do not apply?
 - Visual projection system =/= data coordinate system 
 - Having cut down the number of T. Rexes to just 4, I noticed something strange. 
   From 65 Ma → 70 Ma, the "present-day fossils" of the T. Rexes seem to diverge on different landmasses, whereas their reconstruction - 
   where they were in deep time - stays static near the mid-ocean ridge. 
   We should expect the opposite: present-day fossils to stay in one place as we travel back across time, and reconstructed fossils
   to drift apart.
   If we were playing the animation forward in time, it is reasonable to expect different landmasses, each containing T.rex,
   to collide, so that all the T.rex fossils can be found in the same present-day location, where all three prehistoric landscapes
   converged and smushed together to create the present-day landscape.
   It seems far less likely that the reconstructed fossils simply remained in the SAME LOCATION across deep time, at the bottom of the ocean,
   while their present-day fossils simply drifted apart. The logic doesn't hold up.
   ...which means the dinosaurs in the ocean problem that I've been fretting about...
   may well be a logic error on my part. Perhaps an argument wrongly positioned in my code. 
   To investigate.
   (This was not easy to spot earlier, as my original model before making the museum demo had a lot of moving parts.
    Species phasing in and out of existence depending on when they were alive...
    Over 100-1000 fossils on display at any one time...)

   Meta-lesson: patterns become dificult to spot with the full dataset, full complexity.
   Sometimes a simpler, reduced case (just Tyrannosaurus, and just 4 of them for this demo) can shine a light on what the model
   is or is not doing correctly.

Edit: I found the logic error. It was from setting reconstruction_time = reconstruction_time in the function partition_into_plates. 
      As a result when original lat,lon coordinates were read, they were read at the reconstruction time rather than the present-day.
      Hence the coordinates got "inverted". They were partitioned at the wrong time and therefore their rotations were backward.	

🌊🌊🌊 NO MORE DINOSAURS IN THE OCEANNNN 🌊🌊🌊

🧭 Next steps: 
 - Land to be coloured green, ocean to be coloured blue.
 - Dynamic legend with respect to dinosaur chosen (more coordinate transform headaches)
